figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Integration of RNNs into the LTMLE framework, showing (a) the LSTM architectures (treatment/censoring: two LSTM layers with causally masked self-attention; outcome: one LSTM layer over a 12-month window), (b) the data preprocessing pipeline with feature scaling and per-subject outcome windows, and (c) the integration with TMLE for computing targeted updates.
figures.headline: The diagram shows residual and input-skip connections inside the RNN treatment and outcome networks that feed the targeted update.
citing_sentences: Figure 1 illustrates our approach to integrating RNNs into the LTMLE framework.

Residual connections (labeled “residual” in Figure 1a) add the input of the second LSTM layer and of the attention module to their outputs, so that these layers learn corrections to the representation of the first LSTM layer rather than a new one, which stabilizes the training of the stacked layers.
In all networks, the output of a 16-unit ReLU pre-output layer is concatenated with the current month’s inputs before the output layer (the “input skip” in Figure 1a).

figures.label: Figure A1
figures.caption: Directed acyclic graph (DAG) illustrating the temporal relationships between baseline characteristics ($\mathbf{V}^{1}$, $\mathbf{V}^{2}$, $\mathbf{V}^{3}$), psychiatric ED visits ($\mathbf{L}^{1}_{t}$), metabolic testing ($\mathbf{L}^{2}_{t}$), antidiabetic prescriptions ($\mathbf{L}^{3}_{t}$), treatment ($A_{t}$), censoring ($C_{t}$), and diabetes diagnosis ($Y_{t}$) for $t=0,1,2,3$ ($C_{0}$ and $Y_{0}$ are degenerate and omitted). Arrows represent direct causal effects.
figures.headline: Arrows show each time-varying variable depends on the previous time point, with treatment linked to covariates and diabetes outcome across four time points.
citing_sentences: The data generating process (DGP) is formalized in Appendix A.1 and illustrated by a directed acyclic graph (DAG) in Figure A1, which visualizes complex temporal dependencies across the first four time points.

figures.label: Figure S1
figures.caption: Visualization of treatment adherence patterns and their impact on observed versus counterfactual survival outcomes in a single simulation run with $n=10000$ patients. The stochastic rule assigns a positive probability to every treatment path, so all uncensored patients are compatible with it; its curve in panel (b) (dotted) is therefore the marginal survival curve among uncensored patients in the observed data.
figures.headline: In one simulated run, adherence to the static and dynamic rules declines over time, shown alongside observed and counterfactual survival.
citing_sentences: Figure S1 provides insights into the DGP through a comparative analysis of treatment adherence and survival probability under the treatment rules in a single simulation run.

figures.label: Figure S2
figures.caption: Comparative analysis of RNN– and SL-based estimators over time based on 100 simulation runs with $n=10000$ patients, at target time points $t=12,24,36$. Panel (a) shows the mean absolute bias between true and estimated counterfactual outcomes for each treatment rule. Panel (b) illustrates the coverage probability (proportion of runs) of 95% confidence intervals (dotted line shows nominal level). Panel (c) shows the median confidence interval widths. Results are shown for LTMLE (multi. and bin.), IPTW (multi. and bin.), and G-Comp estimators with SL (solid lines) and RNNs (dashed lines) under static, dynamic, and stochastic treatment rules; g-computation intervals are approximate.
figures.headline: At t=36, multinomial IPTW underestimates risk under static and stochastic rules, with coverage of 0.70 and 0.43.
citing_sentences: Coverage of LTMLE-SL (multi.) ranges from 0.920 under the dynamic rule to 0.973 under the static rule (Table S2), where its intervals are conservative at $t=36$ (Figure 2(b)).
The IPTW-SL estimators perform similarly to LTMLE-SL under the dynamic rule but are biased at later time points under the static and stochastic rules (Figure 2(a)).
IPTW-SL (multi.) underestimates the risk at $t=36$ under the static and stochastic rules, with coverage of 0.70 and 0.43, whereas IPTW-SL (bin.) is less biased (coverage 0.76 and 0.97; Figure 2(b)).

abstract: We propose a doubly-robust method to estimate the causal effects of multi-valued treatment regimes on patient outcomes. A multi-valued treatment regime assigns personalized treatments from a set of competing options based on a patient’s history. Existing methods for optimal treatment regimes are largely limited to binary or continuous treatments. We extend the longitudinal targeted minimum loss-based estimator (LTMLE) to accommodate multi-valued treatments by modeling treatment assignments with a multinomial model. We further integrate recurrent neural networks (RNNs) into the LTMLE framework as learners for the outcome, treatment, and censoring models, and compare this approach to ensemble machine learning. Simulation studies show that LTMLE with either ensemble machine learning or RNNs is approximately unbiased, with close to nominal coverage, whereas sequential g-computation with ensemble machine learning is substantially biased under a dynamic rule. A multinomial treatment model performs similarly to a series of binomial regressions with ensemble machine learning, but yields more stable inference when the treatment model is an RNN.

sections.body: The introduction argues that comparing several competing treatments raises the risk of positivity violations, and that the curse of dimensionality makes sparse treatment sequences more likely as the number of time points grows. It notes that the conventional TMLE approach for multi-valued treatments fits several binary regressions, which can lose efficiency when those models are misspecified. The authors build on a cross-sectional result favouring one multinomial treatment model. They use recurrent neural networks as learners within LTMLE for the outcome, treatment and censoring models. Simulation results are reported in Section 4, with the data-generating process in Appendix A.1.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing targeted estimators handle only binary or continuous treatments, so the paper extends LTMLE to multi-valued treatments with recurrent neural networks.

sections.body: Observational diabetes comparisons of antipsychotics may not adequately control for differences between treatment groups. The motivating study compared several second-generation drugs and one first-generation drug with aripiprazole in a publicly insured U.S. adult population with serious mental illness. It found a reduction in diabetes risk associated with initiating haloperidol, olanzapine, or risperidone relative to aripiprazole. A later bounds analysis found that the lower haloperidol risk held under a substantial share of informative missingness. The section then defines static, dynamic, and stochastic treatment regimes and says the choice among them depends on diagnosis, cardiometabolic risk, and treatment duration.
sections.heading: Motivating example: safety effects of antipsychotic treatment regimes
sections.headline: Earlier antipsychotic comparisons found lower diabetes risk with haloperidol, olanzapine, and risperidone than with aripiprazole.

sections.body: The target is the expected outcome under a treatment rule, identified by the g-formula under consistency, sequential unconfoundedness, and positivity. Two estimators that each rely on one model, sequential g-computation and inverse probability of treatment weighting, serve as comparisons to LTMLE. Treatment and censoring networks are sequence models with two LSTM layers of 32 units, layer normalization, causally masked self-attention, and dropout. Outcome networks use one LSTM layer over the last 12 months. Multinomial treatment models use categorical cross-entropy. Early stopping uses a 10% subject-level validation split.
sections.heading: Doubly-robust estimation
sections.headline: Estimation combines sequential g-computation, inverse probability weighting, and LTMLE, with RNN learners for each nuisance model.

sections.body: Each run simulates 10,000 patients under static, dynamic, and stochastic rules, repeated for 100 simulation runs, with estimates at months 12, 24, and 36. Four metrics are reported: absolute bias, coverage of 95% confidence intervals, interval width, and the proportion of uncensored rule-followers with cumulative probability below 0.025. Table S3 reports that at t=36 this proportion is 0.93 and 0.95 with SL and 0.38 and 0.27 with RNNs under the static and dynamic rules, while the stochastic rule shows no positivity violations. Computation time per run has a median of 25 minutes with RNNs and 56 minutes with SL, so the RNNs were about 2.2 times faster.
sections.heading: Simulations
sections.headline: At month 36, many rule-followers have low cumulative treatment probability under static and dynamic rules, less so with RNNs.

sections.body: The multinomial and binomial specifications perform similarly for LTMLE with ensemble learning. The multinomial model gives more stable inference with RNN treatment models, and the specification also affects IPTW with either learner. Under the dynamic rule, g-computation with ensemble learning is biased by up to 0.059, which the authors attribute to attenuated treatment contrasts across the backward recursion. LTMLE under the dynamic rule is comparable to the static and stochastic rules, apart from lower coverage at later time points. LTMLE-RNN under-covers at t=36 under the stochastic rule, which the authors link to variance estimates from networks fit without cross-fitting.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: A multinomial treatment model gives more stable inference than binomial models when treatment models are RNNs.

sections.body: The conclusion states that LTMLE with either learner is approximately unbiased with close to nominal coverage. It also states that plug-in g-computation under dynamic rules can be badly biased. Two extensions are named. First, positivity violations arise structurally and from sparse data, and fixes such as designing interventions to match observed patterns or truncating density ratios can add their own biases. Second, the authors propose an end-to-end TMLE built on a unified neural network, with cross-fitting, so that propensity estimation is aligned with the target parameter. The paper presents this as future work.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: LTMLE is approximately unbiased in these simulations, and positivity violations and separate propensity fitting remain open problems.

sections.body: The appendix gives the distributions for the simulated data. Race, primary diagnosis, and age are drawn at baseline, with age normal, bounded, and with mean and standard deviation varying by diagnosis. Psychiatric emergency visits follow a negative binomial, and metabolic testing and antidiabetic prescribing are Bernoulli draws. Time-varying equations let these variables depend on prior values and prior treatment, with risperidone giving the largest negative shift in visits. Censoring is deterministic at age 65 and otherwise logistic. Diabetes follows a logistic model with a treatment effect function that differs for risperidone.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix gives the data-generating equations, a causal graph figure, and the treatment-effect definitions.

sections.body: Table S1 lists network and training settings, such as 32 units per LSTM layer, batch size 128, dropout 0.1, and a learning rate of 0.001 for treatment and censoring networks and 0.003 for outcome networks. Definitions S1 to S4 give formulas for absolute bias, coverage, interval width, and low cumulative treatment probability. Table S2 reports performance for each estimator and rule, aggregated over time points. Table S3 gives low-support shares by rule and time. Table S4 gives computation time, with median wall-clock time per run of 56.5 minutes for ensemble learning and 25.2 minutes for RNNs, and totals of 95.3 and 42.8 hours.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Supporting tables give hyperparameters, metric definitions, performance and positivity results, and computation times for each estimator.
